title: How Long Does Public Offer Allotment Take in Nigeria?
summary: After a Nigerian public offer closes, allotment usually takes several weeks. Here is the SEC timeline and when your shares and refund arrive.
body_markdown:
**In short:** After a Nigerian public offer closes, allotment usually takes several weeks. SEC rules require the allotment proposal to be submitted within six weeks of the offer closing, with a possible two-week extension, so four to eight weeks is realistic. Your shares appear in your CSCS account once SEC clears the allotment. Always check the prospectus timetable for the specific dates.


You applied for shares in a public offer, the offer has closed, and now you are refreshing your account waiting for the shares to show up. Nothing is happening, and you are starting to wonder whether something went wrong.


Almost certainly, nothing has. There is a formal process that runs behind the scenes between the day an offer closes and the day shares land in your account, and it takes time. This guide explains how long allotment usually takes, what is happening during the wait, what changes if an offer is oversubscribed or undersubscribed, and when to expect your shares or your refund. If you are new to how the market works overall, our[complete guide to investing in the Nigerian stock market](https://learn.investbamboo.com/how-to-invest-in-the-nigerian-stock-market-ngx-a-complete-beginners-guide/) is a good place to start. Public offers include initial public offerings, so if you are looking specifically at an IPO, our[guide to what an IPO is](https://learn.investbamboo.com/what-is-an-ipo-a-complete-guide-for-nigerian-investors/) covers the fundamentals.


## **How long does public offer allotment take?**


Allotment usually takes several weeks after the offer closes, not days. Under[SEC](https://sec.gov.ng/) rules, the allotment proposal must be submitted to the Commission within six weeks of the close of the issue, and SEC can grant an extension of up to a further two weeks where it judges that necessary.


So a realistic expectation is roughly four to eight weeks before allotment is resolved, and sometimes a little longer once you add the steps that follow, such as publishing the allotment, processing refunds, and crediting shares. The closing date of an offer is not the finish line. It is the point where the subscription window shuts and the back-office work begins.


## **What happens between the offer closing and your shares arriving**


When an offer closes, the issuing house and the other parties to the offer have to turn a pile of applications into a clean register of who gets what. That work is the reason for the wait.


In broad terms, the applications are gathered and reconciled, invalid or incomplete ones are set aside, and the issuing house prepares what is called the basis of allotment, the plan for how shares will be shared out. That plan goes to SEC for review and clearance. Once SEC signs off, the issuer can publish the result, refund any money that is due back, and arrange for the allotted shares to be credited to investors through the Central Securities Clearing System (CSCS). Where the shares are being listed, the listing steps happen around the same time.


Each of those stages takes time, and they happen in sequence rather than all at once. That is why there is a gap, often weeks long, between the offer closing and the shares appearing in your account.


## **What “basis of allotment” means, and what happens if an offer is oversubscribed**


The basis of allotment is simply the formula for sharing out the available shares among everyone who applied. It matters most when an offer is oversubscribed, meaning investors applied for more shares than the company offered.


When that happens, not everyone can get the full number they asked for, so the shares are scaled down according to the agreed formula, subject to SEC clearance. If you applied for 10,000 shares in a heavily oversubscribed offer, you might be allotted 6,000, with the money for the shortfall returned to you.


This is not a rare scenario in the Nigerian market. During the recent wave of bank recapitalisation offers, several were strongly oversubscribed. Fidelity Bank’s 2024 public offer, for example, drew well over a hundred thousand applications and was oversubscribed by more than double its size, which meant the bank and its advisers had to work through a careful allotment before any shares could be credited. Oversubscription is generally a sign of strong investor interest, but for you as an applicant it also means your final allotment may be smaller than what you applied for. We unpack what heavy demand means around a major listing in our piece on[what happens when an IPO is oversubscribed](https://learn.investbamboo.com/what-happens-if-the-dangote-ipo-is-oversubscribed-understanding-ipo-demand-in-nigeria/) .


## **What happens if an offer is undersubscribed**


If an offer attracts less than the shares on offer, what happens next depends on how the offer was structured. Some offers are underwritten, which means an underwriter has agreed in advance to take up some or all of the unsold shares, so the raise can still complete.


If an offer is not underwritten and fails to reach its minimum subscription level, it can be aborted altogether. In that case no shares are issued and applicants get their money back. This is not just theory. In early 2026, Ellah Lakes closed a public offer that[did not meet its minimum subscription and announced it would refund all applicants](https://nairametrics.com/2026/02/22/ellah-lakes-to-refund-investors-after-failed-n235-billion-public-offer/) , with no shares issued, even after extending the subscription window. It is a useful reminder that subscribing to an offer is not a guarantee that you will end up holding the shares.


This is also why the prospectus matters. It sets out the minimum subscription level and the underwriting arrangement, so you know in advance what happens if the offer falls short.


## **When will the shares enter your CSCS account?**


Your shares are credited to your CSCS account after SEC clears the allotment, not on the day the offer closes. It is worth understanding that SEC clearance and CSCS credit are two separate steps. Clearance confirms the basis of allotment, and crediting is the registrar and the depository actually recording the shares against investors’ accounts, which takes additional time after clearance.


The offer timetable in the prospectus usually gives an estimated CSCS credit date, so that is your reference point. On[Bamboo](https://investbamboo.com/nigerian-stocks) , where you can subscribe to public offers directly, you can then track your allotment by checking your CSCS holdings, statement, or dashboard, rather than guessing. You can subscribe straight from your phone, as our[guide to subscribing to an IPO via a mobile app](https://learn.investbamboo.com/can-i-subscribe-to-an-ipo-using-a-mobile-app-in-nigeria/) explains.


## **When should you expect a refund?**


If your application was rejected, or you were allotted fewer shares than you paid for, the extra money should be returned to you. Refunds generally follow once SEC has approved the allotment proposal, and the exact timing depends on the registrar, your payment method, and whether your details were correct.


That last point is the one most within your control. If your bank account details, BVN, name, CSCS number, or CHN were entered incorrectly, your refund or your share credit can be delayed while the mismatch is sorted out. Getting those details right when you apply is the simplest way to avoid a slow refund later.


## **Why allotment sometimes takes longer**


A longer wait does not usually mean something has gone wrong. Allotment can stretch out for several ordinary reasons: the offer drew a very large number of applications, some applications had wrong or missing details, a heavily oversubscribed offer needed a careful allotment formula, the issuing house had reconciliation issues to resolve, SEC asked for corrections or more information, or the refund and crediting steps simply took time to process.


That said, if the wait runs well past the dates given in the offer timetable, it is reasonable to start asking questions rather than waiting indefinitely.


## **What to check, and what to do if your shares do not show up**


Before you subscribe to any offer, read the timetable in the prospectus, and our[guide to reading an IPO prospectus](https://learn.investbamboo.com/how-to-read-an-ipo-prospectus-before-you-invest/) walks through what else to look for. It typically lists the opening and closing dates, the expected allotment date, the SEC clearance date, the refund date, the CSCS credit date, and the listing date, along with the minimum subscription level and whether the offer is underwritten. Those dates tell you what to expect and when it is fair to follow up.


If the expected allotment or CSCS credit date has passed and you still see nothing, first confirm that the offer has actually received SEC clearance, then contact the broker, platform, registrar, or receiving agent you applied through. Have your details ready: your full name, application reference, the amount you paid, the number of shares you applied for, proof of payment, your CSCS number and CHN, and the platform you used. If it stays unresolved, you can escalate to the registrar, the issuing house, or SEC.


## **Frequently asked questions**


**How long does share allotment take after a public offer in Nigeria?** Usually several weeks. SEC rules require the allotment proposal to be submitted within six weeks of the offer closing, with a possible two-week extension, so four to eight weeks is a realistic expectation before allotment is resolved and shares are credited.


**Why have my shares not shown up after the offer closed?** Because allotment is a multi-step process. Applications must be reconciled, the basis of allotment agreed, SEC clearance obtained, and only then are shares credited to CSCS accounts. The prospectus timetable gives the expected dates.


**What happens if a public offer is oversubscribed?** You may receive fewer shares than you applied for, because the available shares are scaled down according to the basis of allotment. The money for the shares you did not get is refunded to you.


**Do I get my money back if an offer fails?** If an offer is not underwritten and does not meet its minimum subscription, it can be aborted, in which case no shares are issued and applicants are refunded. The prospectus sets out the minimum subscription level and refund terms.


**When will I get my refund?** Refunds usually follow after SEC approves the allotment. Timing depends on the registrar and your payment method, and incorrect bank, BVN, CSCS, or CHN details can delay it.

### Quick Summary


This guide explains how long public offer allotment takes in Nigeria. After a public offer closes, the issuer, issuing house, registrar, and SEC must reconcile applications and agree the basis of allotment before shares are issued. Under SEC rules, the allotment proposal must be submitted within six weeks of the close of the offer, with a possible extension of up to two weeks, so investors should realistically expect about four to eight weeks. If an offer is oversubscribed, subscribers may receive fewer shares than they applied for and the balance is refunded. If it is undersubscribed and not underwritten, the offer may be aborted and all money returned. Shares appear in your CSCS account after SEC clears the allotment, and the prospectus timetable is the best guide to the specific dates. This is general information, not investment advice.
